reason: The replication page states that a DELETE naming a version ID deletes that version in the source bucket, does not replicate the deletion to destination buckets, and that this protects data from malicious deletions.
The performance page states scaling happens gradually and is not instantaneous, that 503 (Slow Down) errors may appear while S3 scales to the new rate, and that they dissipate when scaling completes.

Requesters must include x-amz-request-payer as a header or the RequestPayer parameter to accept charges; without the header S3 returns a 403 and charges the bucket owner; context notes bucket owners need not add it.
The page states anonymous access is not allowed once Requester Pays is enabled and that all requests must be authenticated so S3 can identify and charge the requester.
The pricing page says to configure Requester Pays to share data without incurring charges from others' access and that the requester pays request and data transfer costs.
Quote states verbatim that the requester instead of the bucket owner pays for the request and data download, and the bucket owner always pays storage.

The quote, read with the preceding sentence of the same note naming the two groups (Glacier Flexible Retrieval/Deep Archive vs Intelligent-Tiering archive tiers), says one job cannot operate on both types.
The restore page states you can be notified of restore completion with the s3:ObjectRestore:Completed action of S3 Event Notifications.

Both quoted sentences state the Glacier FR/DA restored copies are kept only for the days specified, while Intelligent-Tiering archive tier restores have no expiration and move back to Frequent Access.

Quote under the Glacier FR/DA archival heading says archived objects are not accessible in real time, a restore yields a temporary copy for the duration specified, and the storage class remains Glacier FR or DA.

The Bulk bullet calls it the lowest-cost retrieval option and the quote gives typical 5-12 hours for Flexible Retrieval, 48 hours for Deep Archive, and free Bulk for Flexible Retrieval and Intelligent-Tiering.

The Expedited bullet (Flexible Retrieval or IT Archive Access) says occasional urgent requests, objects under 250 MB typically within 1-5 minutes, premium feature per the note; the table row shows Not available for Deep Archive.
Quote states Standard is the default when no option is specified, typically 3-5 hours for Flexible Retrieval and within 12 hours for Deep Archive.
Quote advises tracking throughput and retrying the slowest 5 percent for large variably sized requests, for example more than 128 MB.
Quotes give the guideline to retry a GET or PUT after 2 seconds for smaller requests (less than 512 KB) and a second retry after an additional 4 seconds.
The RTC page says it replicates most objects in seconds and 99.9 percent of those objects within 15 minutes.
Quotes state replication metrics and replication events are available within 15 minutes of enabling S3 RTC, and enabling RTC also enables replication metrics on the rule.

Quotes state the RTC SLA does not apply when request-per-second performance guidelines are exceeded or when the replication transfer rate exceeds the default 1 Gbps quota; context says the quota can be raised.
Quote states Metrics:EventThreshold:Minutes and ReplicationTime:Time:Minutes can only have 15 as a valid value.
Quota table row: Replication transfer rate, each account 1 Gigabits per second, adjustable Yes, described as the maximum RTC transfer rate from the source region in this account.
Quote states that when the bucket owner and the user's parent account are the same, the owner can use either a bucket policy or a user policy to grant access.

Quotes state server access logging gives detailed request records that assist security and access audits, and CloudTrail data events record object-level API activity for individual buckets such as GetObject, DeleteObject and PutObject.
Quotes state S3 encrypts objects before saving them on disks and decrypts on download, and with client-side encryption you encrypt before upload and manage the process, keys and tools.
Quote states updates to a single key are atomic and a concurrent GET during a PUT returns old or new data, never partial or corrupt data.
Quotes support a single PUT up to 5 GB and multipart up to 50 TB, but do not state that larger objects need multipart; the same list offers console upload of a single object up to 160 GB.
Quote states latency-sensitive applications can achieve consistent small-object (and first-byte-out for larger objects) latencies of roughly 100-200 milliseconds.
Quotes state SRR has no data transfer charges and CRR inter-Region data transfer charges vary depending on the Regions chosen.

Quotes state that starting April 2026 SSE-C is disabled by default for new general purpose buckets and existing buckets in accounts with no SSE-C objects, and is enabled by setting BlockedEncryptionTypes to NONE via PutBucketEncryption.

Quote states SSE-C needs the key with every read or write request, making sharing impractical, AWS managed services cannot natively decrypt SSE-C objects, and SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS give equivalent protection with greater flexibility.
Quotes state S3 never stores the SSE-C key, you must supply it for every download, and you must use HTTPS when specifying SSE-C headers.
FAQ quotes state KMS manages the keys, adds separate permissions for using the KMS key, and provides an audit trail of who used the key for which object and when, including failed attempts.

Quotes and the bullet between them in the cross-account section state aws/s3 is used when no key is named, it can be used by principals in the key's account, and cross-account access calls for a customer managed key whose policy allows the other account.
Quote states verbatim that with SSE-KMS on an S3 bucket the KMS keys must be in the same Region as the bucket.
Quote states multi-Region KMS keys can be used but S3 treats them as single-Region keys and does not use their multi-Region features.
Quote, following the SSE-S3 default sentence, says to choose SSE-KMS or DSSE-KMS if you need more control over keys such as key rotation and access policy grants.

Quotes state every bucket has encryption by default with SSE-S3, new objects are encrypted at rest, other types can be named in PUT (SSE-KMS, DSSE-KMS, SSE-C) or set as bucket default (SSE-KMS or DSSE-KMS).
Under 'We recommend the following', Standard-IA is for the primary or only copy of data that can't be re-created, and Standard-IA objects are resilient to the loss of an Availability Zone.
Quotes give the Standard-IA and One Zone-IA recommendations (including CRR replicas) and state One Zone-IA stores data in one AZ and is not resilient to the physical loss of that AZ.

FAQ quotes state SCA monitors object-level access patterns within an individual bucket/prefix/tag for the previous 30-90 days, recommends a storage class, and you then configure an S3 Lifecycle policy.
Quotes state each object has a storage class, and if none is specified on upload S3 assigns S3 Standard, the default.
